are the
X
and
Z
check matrices respectively.

X_{3}
corresponds to the
meta-checks
of the
Z
-stabilizer (or
X
-error) syndrome, which makes the 3D color code single-shot decodable, and
d_{2}^{T}
is the associated meta-check matrix.

Similarly, color cohomology is a convenient language to describe twisted color circuits, such as the one in Section
II
.
For example, the configuration of
Z
measurement results can be mapped to a color 2-cochain, and the configuration of
X
results to a color 1-cycle.
Therefore, color cohomology turns out to be the natural language to formulate the decoding of twisted color circuits, as we do in Section
V
.

III.3
Color cohomology: Equivalence to cellular cohomology

In this section, we show that color cohomology is equivalent to three copies of cellular cohomology (or in other words, to cellular cohomology with coefficient group
\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{3}
).
Technically, we show that there is a chain map
M
from color to cellular cohomology, as defined around Eq. (
36
).
Importantly, all
M_{i}
are
local
meaning that the matrix entries are only non-zero for neighboring pairs of cells, and the chain map corresponds to an isomorphism (not just a homomorphism) of cohomology groups.
A chain map very similar to
M
was used in Ref.
[
30
]
to show the equivalence between the 3+1D color code and three copies of the 3+1D toric code.

2D —

As usual, we will start with the analogous 2D case, and give a chain map
M_{i}
from 2D color cohomology to
\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{2}
-valued (not
\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{3}
-valued) cellular cohomology.
The 2-cellulation on which the cellular
i
-chains are defined is just the 2-colex with the coloring removed.
More precisely, we define one map
M_{i}^{c}
for every
c\in\{r,g,b\}
from color
i
-chains to
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
-valued cellular
i
-chains, such that
M_{i}
can be built from taking any two of the three
M_{i}^{c}
, while the third
M_{i}^{c}
is redundant.
The
M_{i}^{c}
are given by

\displaystyle(M_{-1}^{c})_{0\kappa}

\displaystyle\coloneqq\delta_{c\in\kappa}\;,

\displaystyle(M_{0}^{c})_{pf}

\displaystyle\coloneqq\delta_{\mathbf{c}_{f}=c}\partial_{pf}\;,

(55)

\displaystyle(M_{1}^{c})_{ep}

\displaystyle\coloneqq\delta_{\mathbf{c}_{e}=\overline{c}}\partial_{ep}\;,

\displaystyle(M_{2}^{c})_{f^{\prime}f}

\displaystyle\coloneqq\delta_{\mathbf{c}_{f}\neq c}\partial_{f^{\prime}f}\;,

\displaystyle(M_{3}^{c})_{0\kappa}

\displaystyle\coloneqq\delta_{c\in\kappa}\;,

and illustrated in Fig.
15
.

Figure 15:

Action of
M_{i}^{r}
or
(M_{i}^{r})^{T}
on color chains formed by a single generator.
Note that
(M_{2}^{r})^{T}=(M_{2}^{r})
.
Permuting colors yields analogous illustrations for
M_{i}^{g}
and
M_{i}^{b}
.

Let us now check that Eq. (
36
) indeed holds for some cases.
For
i=0
, we have

\sum_{p\in\Delta_{0}}\partial_{ep}\delta_{\mathbf{c}_{f}=c}\partial_{pf}=\sum_{p\in\Delta_{0}}\delta_{\mathbf{c}_{e}=\overline{c}}\partial_{ep}\partial_{pf}\;.

(56)

We confirm this by going through the different cases.
If
\mathbf{c}_{f}\neq c
and
\mathbf{c}_{e}\neq\overline{c}
, both sides are immediately zero.
If
\mathbf{c}_{f}\neq c
and
\mathbf{c}_{e}=\overline{c}
, the left-hand side is zero immediately.
The right-hand side is zero as well, since any
\overline{c}
-colored edge
e
either shares no vertex with a non-
c
-colored face
f
, or
e\subset f
and they share two vertices.
If
\mathbf{c}_{f}=c
and
\mathbf{c}_{e}\neq\overline{c}
, the right-hand is zero immediately.
The left-hand side is zero as well, since any non-
\overline{c}
-colored edge
e
either shares no vertex with a
c
-colored face, or
e\subset f
and they share two vertices.
Finally, if
\mathbf{c}_{f}=c
and
\mathbf{c}_{e}=\overline{c}
, both sides are immediately identical.
For
i=1
, we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\sum_{e\in\Delta_{1}}\partial_{fe}\delta_{\mathbf{c}_{e}=\overline{c}}\partial_{ep}=&\sum_{f^{\prime}\in\Delta_{2}}\delta_{\mathbf{c}_{f}\neq c}\partial_{ff^{\prime}}\partial_{f^{\prime}p}\\
=&\delta_{\mathbf{c}_{f}\neq c}\partial_{fp}\;.\end{split}

(57)

We confirm this equation again by going through the different cases.
If
\mathbf{c}_{f}=c
, then the right-hand side is immediately zero.
The left-hand side is zero as well since there are no edges of color
\overline{c}
in the boundary of the face
f
.
If
\mathbf{c}_{f}\neq c
, then both sides are
1
if
p\in f
, and both sides are zero if
p\not\in f
.

Finally, we note that
\overline{M}\coloneqq M^{T}
defines a chain map from transposed cellular cohomology to color cohomology.
This is because color cohomology is symmetric under transposition,
d_{i}=d_{1-i}^{T}
.

3D —

Having discussed the equivalence between color and cellular cohomology in 2D, the generalization to 3D is straight-forward:
We start by defining one chain map
M^{c}
for every
c\in\mathcal{C}
from color to
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
-valued cellular cohomology, such that
M
can be constructed from any triple, while the fourth
M^{c}
is redundant.
The
M_{i}^{c}
are given by

\displaystyle(M_{-1}^{c})_{0\kappa}

\displaystyle\coloneqq\delta_{c\in\kappa}\;,

\displaystyle(M_{0}^{c})_{pv}

\displaystyle\coloneqq\delta_{\mathbf{c}_{v}=c}\partial_{pv}\;,

(58)

\displaystyle(M_{1}^{c})_{ep}

\displaystyle\coloneqq\delta_{\mathbf{c}_{e}=\overline{c}}\partial_{ep}\;,

\displaystyle(M_{2}^{c})_{f^{\prime}f}

\displaystyle\coloneqq\delta_{c\not\in\mathbf{c}_{f}}\partial_{f^{\prime}f}\;,

\displaystyle(M_{3}^{c})_{v^{\prime},(v,c^{\prime})}

\displaystyle\coloneqq\delta_{c=c^{\prime}}\partial_{v^{\prime}v}\;,

\displaystyle(M_{4}^{c})_{0c^{\prime}}

\displaystyle\coloneqq\delta_{c=c^{\prime}}\;.

Let us verify Eq. (
36
).
For
i=-1
, we have

\delta_{c\in\kappa}=\sum_{v\in\Delta_{3}}\delta_{\mathbf{c}_{v}=c}\partial_{pv}\delta_{\mathbf{c}_{v}\in\kappa}=\delta_{c\in\kappa}\sum_{v\in\Delta_{3}}\delta_{\mathbf{c}_{v}=c}\partial_{pv}\;.

(59)

The equation holds because the sum on the right is the number of
c
-colored volumes adjacent to the vertex
p
, which is always
1
.
For
i=0
, we have

\sum_{p\in\Delta_{0}}\partial_{ep}\delta_{\mathbf{c}_{v}=c}\partial_{pv}=\sum_{p\in\Delta_{0}}\delta_{\mathbf{c}_{e}=\overline{c}}\partial_{ep}\partial_{pv}\;.

(60)

If
\mathbf{c}_{v}\neq c
and
\mathbf{c}_{e}\neq\overline{c}
, both sides are zero immediately.
If
\mathbf{c}_{v}=c
and
\mathbf{c}_{e}\neq\overline{c}
, the left-hand side is zero immediately.
The right-hand side is zero as well because
e
shares either no vertex with the
c
-colored volume
v
, or
e\subset v
and they share 2 vertices.
The case
\mathbf{c}_{v}\neq c
and
\mathbf{c}_{e}=\overline{c}
is the same up to color permutation.
If
\mathbf{c}_{v}=c
and
\mathbf{c}_{e}=\overline{c}
, both sides are identical immediately.
For
i=1
, we have

\sum_{e\in\Delta_{1}}\partial_{fe}\delta_{\mathbf{c}_{e}=\overline{c}}\partial_{ep}=\sum_{f^{\prime}\in\Delta_{2}}\delta_{c\not\in\mathbf{c}_{f}}\partial_{ff^{\prime}}\partial_{f^{\prime}p}=\delta_{c\not\in\mathbf{c}_{f}}\partial_{fp}\;.

(61)

If
c\in\mathbf{c}_{f}
, the right-hand side is zero immediately.
The left-hand side is zero as well since the
\mathbf{c}_{f}
-colored face
f
has no
\overline{c}
-colored edges.
If
c\not\in\mathbf{c}_{f}
, then both sides are
1
if
p\in f
, and both sides are zero if
p\not\in f
.
For
i=2
, we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\partial_{vf}\delta_{c\not\in\mathbf{c}_{f}}=&\sum_{f^{\prime}\in\Delta_{2}}\partial_{vf^{\prime}}\delta_{c\not\in\mathbf{c}_{f}}\partial_{f^{\prime}f}\\
=&\sum_{v^{\prime}\in\Delta_{3},c^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}}\delta_{c=c^{\prime}}\partial_{vv^{\prime}}\delta_{c^{\prime}\not\in\mathbf{c}_{f}}\partial_{v^{\prime}f}=\delta_{c\not\in\mathbf{c}_{f}}\partial_{vf}\;,\end{split}

(62)

and both sides are identical immediately.
For
i=3
, we have

\sum_{v^{\prime}\in\Delta_{3}}\delta_{c=c^{\prime}}\partial_{vv^{\prime}}=\sum_{c^{\prime\prime}\in\mathcal{C}}\delta_{c=c^{\prime\prime}}\delta_{c^{\prime}=c^{\prime\prime}}\;,

(63)

which holds immediately.

We can also define a reverse chain map
\overline{M}
from (
\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{3}
-valued) cellular cohomology to color cohomology.
More precisely, we can define one chain map
\overline{M}^{\kappa}
for each color pair
\kappa\in\mathcal{C}_{2}
.
Any triple of color pairs
\kappa
that cover all four colors can be combined into
\overline{M}
, while the other three chain maps are redundant.
The 3-cellulation is obtained from the 3-colex as follows:
The cellulation vertices are at the centers of the 3-colex volumes
v
whose color is in
\kappa
,
\mathbf{c}_{v}\in\kappa
.
The cellulation edges are dual to the 3-colex faces
f
of color
\mathbf{c}_{f}=\kappa
, connecting the vertices at the centers of the volumes adjacent to
f
.
The cellulation faces are the 3-colex faces of opposite color
\overline{\kappa}
, which are enlarged such that their vertices are at the centers of the adjacent
\mathbf{c}_{v}\in\kappa
volumes.
The cellulation volumes are the 3-colex volumes
v
of color
\mathbf{c}_{v}\notin\kappa
, again enlarged.
So for each cellulation cell
c
, there is an associated 3-colex cell, which we denote by
x(c)
.

Now,
\overline{M}^{\kappa}
is defined as follows:

\displaystyle(\overline{M}_{-1}^{\kappa})_{\kappa^{\prime}0}

\displaystyle\coloneqq\delta_{\kappa=\kappa^{\prime}}\;,

\displaystyle(\overline{M}_{0}^{\kappa})_{vp}

\displaystyle\coloneqq\delta_{v=x(p)}\;,

(64)

\displaystyle(\overline{M}_{1}^{\kappa})_{pe}

\displaystyle\coloneqq\partial_{p,x(e)}\;,

\displaystyle(\overline{M}_{2}^{\kappa})_{f^{\prime}f}

\displaystyle\coloneqq\delta_{f^{\prime}=x(f)}\;,

\displaystyle(\overline{M}_{3}^{\kappa})_{(v^{\prime},c)v}

\displaystyle\coloneqq\delta_{v^{\prime}=x(v)}\delta_{c\in\kappa}\;,

\displaystyle(\overline{M}_{4}^{\kappa})_{c0}

\displaystyle\coloneqq\delta_{c\in\kappa}\;.

Physically, the equivalence between the two cohomology theories implies that the codes or circuits built from both can be understood as different microscopic realizations of the same topological phase.
For example, mappings
M
and
\overline{M}
define local isometries between the 3D color code (which is based on 3D color cohomology) and three copies of the toric code (each based on 3D cellular cohomology), which show that they are in the same topological phase.
We will later use the cohomology equivalence in Section
IV.3
to show that the color path integral represents a particular non-Abelian topological phase.

IV
The color path integral as a non-Abelian phase

In Section
II
, we motivated the color path integral in terms of a 3+0D protocol based on the 3D color code.
In this section, we will give a more natural and direct physical interpretation of the path integral, namely as a spacetime fixed-point model for a 2+1D non-Abelian topological phase.
To this end, we introduce a state-sum language for general path integrals in Section
IV.1
, after which the color path integral can be conveniently described in terms of color cohomology in Section
IV.2
.
Using the cohomology equivalence from Section
III.3
, we then show in Section
IV.3
that the color path integral is equivalent to a known model for a non-Abelian phase, namely the Dijkgraaf-Witten state sum for the type-
III
group 3-cocycle on
\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{3}
.
In Section
IV.4
, we equip the path integral with flux and charge defect configurations, which is necessary to turn its tensor network representation into a fault-tolerant circuit.
Finally, in Section
IV.5
, we discuss how to equip the path integral with boundaries.

IV.1
Discrete path integrals

Before we get to the color path integral, we introduce path integrals more generally, and explain how they describe topological phases.
We introduce their
fixed-point
property, which implies that isolated errors do not affect the logical action of the circuit.
One way to define a path integral is as a tensor network with tensors assigned to certain places of a spacetime lattice, and index contractions between nearby tensors.
We have defined the color path integral in this way in Section
II.2
.
For this section it will be more convenient to use an alternative, but equivalent, language to describe path integrals, which in the context of topological phases is known as
state sums

[
47
,
48
,
49
,
50
,
51
,
52
,
53
]
.

State-sum path integrals —

A
state-sum path integral
associates variables to certain places of the spacetime lattice, such as all the vertices, all the edges, or all the corners of volumes.
The variables take values in some finite set, such as
\{0,1\}
.
Evaluating the path “integral” means summing over all spacetime configurations
\vec{c}
of the variables.
The summand is a product of weights
\omega_{x}
, which are also associated to certain places
x
of the spacetime lattice.
These weights are complex numbers
\omega
that depend on the configuration of the variables within some constant-size neighborhood.
So, schematically, a state-sum path integral can be written as

Z=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{confs. }\vec{c}\ \end{subarray}}\prod_{\text{places }x}\omega_{x}(\vec{c}|_{\text{near }x})\;.

(65)

The path integrals we consider are uniform, that is, the distribution of variables and weights only depends on what the lattice looks like locally.
In particular, on a translation-invariant spacetime lattice the path integral is translation invariant as well, and specified by a single unit cell.
In physics, state sums are commonly used in statistical mechanics, where they are referred to as “partition functions”.
For example, the classical 2D Ising model at inverse temperature
\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{+}
is a state sum on a 2D square lattice, with one
\{\pm 1\}
-valued variable at each vertex, and one “Boltzmann” weight
\omega_{e}(c)=e^{-\beta Jc(e_{0})c(e_{1})}
at each edge
e
with endpoints
e_{0}
and
e_{1}
.

Let us briefly point out how state sums are equivalent to tensor networks.
A tensor network is evaluated by summing over all configurations of contracted index pairs.
The summand is the product over all tensor entries for the corresponding index configuration.
So the contracted index pairs in the tensor network are equivalent to the variables in the state sum, and the tensors themselves are equivalent to the weights.
State sums may seem more general, as an index contraction can only involve two indices, whereas a variable can enter into an arbitrary number of weights.
However, we can define the contraction over a larger number of indices by connecting them all to one common
Kronecker
\delta
-tensor
, which is the generalization of the
Z
-tensor in Eq. (
5
) to arbitrary bond dimensions.

Evaluating the path integral on a closed spacetime lattice with periodic boundary conditions yields a number
Z
as in Eq. (
65
).
This number is not particularly relevant for our purposes.
What is relevant instead is the evaluation of the path integral on a spacetime lattice with
state boundaries
.
In this case, we freeze a configuration
\vec{c}_{\text{boundary}}
of state-sum variables within a constant distance from the boundary, and sum over all other variables in the interior.
This way, we get a vector of numbers
Z(\vec{c}_{\text{boundary}})
, instead of a single number, which can be interpreted as the state vector of a state defined on degrees of freedom living on the boundary.
13
13

13

If we divide the boundary into an
input
and an
output
component, the state can also be interpreted as a vectorized linear map from the input to the output vector space.

For a tensor-network path integral, this corresponds to cutting the indices near the boundary and leaving them open.

Physical interpretation of path integrals —

The path integrals that we consider are defined in a 3D spacetime and describe the zero-temperature physics of a 2D quantum model, in contrast to thermal physics for the Ising-model path integral illustrated above.
So our path integrals can be viewed as an alternative language to 2D lattice Hamiltonians.
14
14

14

Physically, our path integrals have the same qualitative properties as the imaginary-time evolution of a 2D Hamiltonian
[
52
]
.
It should be noted though, that our path integrals are defined in discrete time, whereas the imaginary-time evolution is defined in continuous time.
One could in principle obtain a path integral from an imaginary-time evolution by Trotterization, but our path integrals do not directly arise in this way.

The state
Z(\vec{c}_{\text{boundary}})
then plays a role analogous to the ground state of a Hamiltonian model.

In particular, we consider path integrals that represent non-trivial 2D topological phases.
15
15

15

Note that topological phases can be defined directly on the level of path integrals:
Two path integrals are in the same phase if they are related by a continuous deformation that does maintain a constant spectral gap of the transfer operator (corresponding to a 2D layer of the 3D path integral).
We believe that the resulting classification of topological phases is closely related to that for lattice Hamiltonians.

While lattice Hamiltonians are more commonly used to describe topological phases in condensed-matter physics, the path-integral language makes it easier to construct syndrome-extraction circuits for these topological phases.
More precisely, our path integrals are directly equal to a syndrome-extraction circuit that is post-selected onto a particular (
+1
) outcome.
In this context,
Z(\vec{c}_{\text{boundary}})
corresponds to a code state of an underlying error correcting code.
This code will, in general, be microscopically different depending on the chosen state boundary but is guaranteed to inherit necessary properties for error correction from the path integral.

Fixed-point path integrals —

We use a strongly restricted subclass of path integrals, which are particularly useful for constructing error-correcting circuits.
Namely, we use ones that represent the desired topological phase in a particularly pure manner, at zero correlation length.
We call them
fixed-point
path integrals
[
52
,
53
]
, and define them in the following.
Consider evaluating the path integral on a 3-ball with a smaller 3-ball removed from its center.
We consider both interior and exterior boundary 2-spheres as state boundaries, and assume that they are separated by at least some constant lattice distance
d_{0}
.
16
16

16

For usual examples,
d_{0}
is very small, for example it might suffice if the interior and exterior are separated by at least one lattice edge.

Evaluating the path integral on this lattice yields a state
\ket{T}
on the boundary, which can be considered a bipartite state where one part corresponds to the interior boundary and the other to the exterior boundary.
The defining property of a fixed-point path integral is that
\ket{T}
is a product state,
\ket{T}=\ket{T_{in}}\otimes\ket{T_{out}}
, as illustrated by following 2D toy picture:

\langle O_{0}O_{1}\rangle-\langle O_{0}\rangle\langle O_{1}\rangle
.

(68)

The fixed-point property in Eq. (
66
) is the underlying reason why the circuits that we construct from the path integral have a fault-tolerant threshold:
If we view the inserted operator
O
as an error, then this means that isolated errors are irrelevant.

Note that typical examples of fixed-point path integrals have nice algebraic properties, such as an exact notion of topological invariance.
That is, we can freely deform the underlying spacetime lattice by locally applying
rewrite rules
, which are equations between small tensor networks, such as the
ZX
rules
[
52
,
53
,
27
]
.
Similarly, if two fixed-point path integrals are in the same topological phase, then they are typically related via local rewrite rules as well.

Boundaries and other defects —

The state boundaries discussed above are to be contrasted with
physical boundaries
, which we have discussed in Section
II.4
and will revisit in Section
IV.5
.
The main difference is that for physical boundaries we do sum over all boundary variables instead of keeping them fixed.
To define a physical boundary, we do not only remove the variables outside the boundary and the weights depending on them, but we may also introduce new variables and weights on the boundary.
18
18

18

Since we sum over all boundary variables, evaluating the path integral with physical boundary yields again a number
Z
.
We can also evaluate the path integral on a lattice whose boundary is divided into a physical-boundary part and a state-boundary part, yielding a state supported only on the state-boundary part.
In this case, the state itself has a physical boundary, which is the region separating state and physical boundary in spacetime.

In the tensor-network language, a physical boundary is a way to close off the open indices obtained from merely cutting the tensor network along some surface (corresponding to a state boundary).
Similarly, we can consider
domain walls
, which are 2D surfaces separating two different 3D regions where the path integral is defined differently, one on each side.

Boundaries and domain walls for the path integral are needed to construct a protocol with a globally planar layout, which implements a non-Clifford logic gate.
Eq. (
1
) shows an example of a configuration of boundaries and domain walls that corresponds to a particular logic operation.
Like the topological phases for the bulk, the different physical boundaries (or domain walls) can be classified into different
boundary phases
.
The logical action of the resulting circuit only depends on the topological phases of the bulk, boundaries, and domain walls in the spacetime diagram.
The boundaries and domain walls we consider are such that they obey the fixed-point property in Eq. (
66
) also on the boundary or domain wall.

In a conceptually similar way, we can equip a path integral with
cohomological defects
as in Section
IV.4
.
That is, in addition to the variables, we let the weights depend on some cohomological chain (see Section
III.1
), which we do not sum over.
Such cohomological chains represent the configurations of measurement outcomes of the circuit.

IV.2
The color path integral via color cohomology

In this section, we reintroduce the color path integral from Section
II.2
, formulated as a state sum using color cohomology.
We first introduce the 2D analog of the 3D color path integral, both for pedagogical reasons and because we will use it later to show an important property (“gauge invariance”) of the 3D color path integral.

2D —

The
2D untwisted color path integral
is defined on any 2-colex as

Z_{\text{untw}}=\sum_{A\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\Delta_{0}}}\prod_{f\in\Delta_{2}}\delta_{(dA)_{f}=0}=\sum_{A\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\Delta_{0}}:dA=0}1\;.

(69)

This is a state sum with one
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
-valued variable at every vertex, and one weight at every face
f
enforcing that
(dA)_{f}=0
, where
d=d_{1}
is the coboundary of 2D color cohomology, see Section
III.2
.
As shown, this weight can be suppressed by summing only over 2D color 1-cocycles
A
.
The
2D (twisted) color path integral
includes an additional weight at every vertex
p\in\Delta_{0}
:

Z=\sum_{A\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\Delta_{0}}:dA=0}\prod_{p\in\Delta_{0}}e^{\sgn_{p}\frac{2\pi i}{4}\overline{A_{p}}}\;.

(70)

Here,
\sgn_{p}=+1
if cycling through the adjacent faces in the ordering
r-g-b
is clockwise, and
\sgn_{p}=-1
otherwise.
Also,
\overline{A_{t}}
means that we consider
A_{t}
as an element of
\mathbb{Z}
instead of
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
.
The overall weight is the exponential of the following
action
:

S[A]=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{p\in\Delta_{0}}\sgn_{p}\overline{A_{p}}\mod 1\in\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}\;.

(71)

The central property of the action is its
gauge invariance
,

A^{\prime}\coloneqq A+d\alpha\quad\Rightarrow\quad S[A^{\prime}]=S[A]\;,

(72)

for any 2D color 1-cocycle
A
and color 0-cochain
\alpha
.
Gauge invariance directly implies that
S
only depends on the cohomology class of the color 1-cocycle
A
.
It suffices to show gauge invariance for the generating 0-chains
\alpha=f
formed by a single face
f
.
We indeed find:

\displaystyle\begin{split}S[A^{\prime}]-S[A]=&\frac{1}{4}\sum_{p\in\Delta_{0}}\sgn_{p}(\overline{A_{p}+(df)_{p}}-\overline{A_{p}})\\
\overset{\eqref{eq:integer_lift_expansion}}{=}&\frac{1}{4}\sum_{p\in\Delta_{0}}\sgn_{p}\big(\overline{(df)_{p}}+2\overline{A_{p}}\overline{(df)_{p}})\big)\\
\overset{*}{=}&\frac{1}{4}\sum_{p\in f}\sgn_{p}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{p\in f}\overline{A_{p}}\overset{**}{=}\frac{1}{2}\overline{(dA)_{f}}\\
=&0\;.\end{split}

(73)

For the middle equality, we have used that

\overline{a+b}-\overline{a}=\overline{b}-2\overline{a}\overline{b}

(74)

for
a,b\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}
.
For (
*
) we have used that the summand is only supported on the vertices
p\in f
.
For (
**
) we have used that the first summand is zero, since the 3-colorability implies that
f
has an equal number of vertices
p\in f
with
\sgn_{p}=1
and
\sgn_{p}=-1
.
We have also used the definition of
d_{1}
and that
A
is a color 1-cocycle.
Finally, we note that the action in Eq. (
71
) (or better, the according weight in Eq. (
70
)) is analogous to the transversal
S
gate in the 2D color code, and the gauge invariance is analogous to the fact that the transversal gate preserves the code space.

3D —

After describing the 2D color path integral, the 3D generalization is rather straight-forward.
The
(3D) untwisted color path integral
is defined on any 3-colex as

Z_{\text{untw}}=\sum_{A\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\Delta_{0}}}\prod_{f\in\Delta_{2}}\delta_{(dA)_{f}=0}=\sum_{A\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\Delta_{0}}:dA=0}1\;.

(75)

The
(3D twisted) color path integral
includes an additional weight:

Z=\sum_{A\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\Delta_{0}}:dA=0}\prod_{p\in\Delta_{0}}e^{\sgn_{p}\frac{2\pi i}{8}\overline{A_{p}}}\;,

(76)

recalling the sign
\sgn_{p}
of a vertex
p
from the beginning of Section
II.2
.

Let us briefly confirm that this is indeed the same as the color path integral introduced in Section
II.2
as a
ZX
tensor network.
Indeed, the weight
\delta_{(dA)_{f}=0}
at a face
f
is
1
if the variables at all the vertices of
p\in f
sum to
0\operatorname{mod}2
, and
0
otherwise.
So these weights correspond to the
X
tensors at every face in Fig.
1
.
The summation over the variable at every vertex corresponds to a “multi-index contraction”, which is implemented by a
Z
-tensor with indices connected to all adjacent face weights.
The state-sum weight
e^{\sgn_{p}\frac{2\pi i}{8}\overline{A_{p}}}
at every vertex
p
is implemented by adding a phase of
\sgn_{p}\frac{2\pi}{8}
to the according
Z
-tensor in the tensor network.

The overall weight in the path integral is the exponential of the following action:

S[A]=\frac{1}{8}\sum_{p\in\Delta_{0}}\sgn_{p}\overline{A_{p}}\;.

(77)

The action is again gauge invariant as defined in Eq. (
72
), and thus only depends on the cohomology class of
A
.
In the 3D case, gauge invariance ensures that the resulting path integral is a fixed-point path integral and obeys the zero-correlation length condition in Eq. (
66
).
It suffices to show gauge invariance for the generating 0-cochains
\alpha=v
consisting of a single volume
v\in\Delta_{3}
.
We indeed find:

\displaystyle\begin{split}S[A^{\prime}]-S[A]=&\frac{1}{8}\sum_{p\in\Delta_{0}}\sgn_{p}(\overline{A_{p}+(dv)_{p}}-\overline{A_{p}})\\
\overset{\eqref{eq:integer_lift_expansion}}{=}&\frac{1}{8}\sum_{p\in\Delta_{0}}\sgn_{p}\big(\overline{(dv)_{p}}+2\overline{A_{p}}\overline{(dv)_{p}})\big)\\
=&\frac{1}{8}\sum_{p\in v}\sgn_{p}+\frac{1}{4}\sum_{p\in v}\sgn_{p}\overline{A_{p}}\\
\overset{*}{=}&S_{\text{2D},v}[A|_{v}]=0\;.\end{split}

(78)

For (
*
) we have used that due to the 4-colorability the number of
\sgn_{p}=+1
and
\sgn_{p}=-1
vertices of
v
is equal, so the first summand vanishes.
We have also used that the second term is the action
S_{\text{2D},v}
of the 2D color path integral restricted to the boundary of
v
, which is a 2-colex when colored according to the adjacent volumes.
Since (1) the color 1-cohomology group on any 2-sphere is trivial and (2) the 2D action is gauge invariant and only depends on the 1-cohomology class, the 2D action is the same as for the
A=0
color 1-cocycle, namely
0
.
Finally, we note that the action in Eq. (
77
) (or better, the corresponding phase factor in Eq. (
76
)) is the same as occurs in the transversal
T
gate of the 3D color code.

IV.3
Equivalence to type-III twisted path integral

In this section, we establish that the color path integral represents a non-Abelian topological phase.
We will do this by showing its equivalence to a known path integral, namely the
Dijkgraaf-Witten
state sum
[
50
]
for the group
\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{3}
and the type-III group 3-cocycle.
The latter is known to host a non-Abelian anyon theory
[
54
]
.
This equivalence is an extension of the equivalence between color and cellular cohomology discussed in Section
III.3
.

2D cellular path integral —

As usual, we start with a simpler 2D analogy of the 3D equivalence.
We show the equivalence of the 2D twisted color path integral with the following
2D twisted cellular path integral
, defined on any 2-cellulation:

\begin{multlined}Z_{\text{cell}}=\sum_{A_{r},A_{g}\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\Delta_{1}}}\prod_{f\in\Delta_{2}}\delta_{(d^{\text{cell}}A_{r})_{f}=0}\;\delta_{(d^{\text{cell}}A_{g})_{f}=0}\\
\times\prod_{f\in\Delta_{2}}e^{2\pi i\frac{1}{2}(A_{r}\cup A_{g})(f)}\;.\end{multlined}

(79)

So the path integral is the sum over all pairs of (cellular) 1-cocycles
A_{r}
and
A_{g}
, with an action

S[A_{r},A_{g}]=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{f\in\Delta_{2}}(A_{r}\cup A_{g})(f)\;.

(80)

Here
\cup
denotes the
cup product
, whose value on a face
f
only depends on the values of
A_{r}
and
A_{g}
on the edges of
f
.
There are explicit formulas for the cup product on triangulations
[
55
]
, cubulations
[
56
]
or general cellulations
[
28
]
.
Intuitively, the cup product counts the number of intersections of the closed-loop patterns
A_{r}
and
A_{g}
.
To turn this intuition into a concrete formula, we divide the edges
e
of the face
f
with
(A_{r})_{e}=1
into pairs in an arbitrary way.
Then, we connect the two edge centers of each edge pair with a red line.
Analogously, we connect the
(A_{g})_{e}=1
edge centers with green lines.

(A_{r}\cup A_{g})(f)
is then given by the
\operatorname{mod}2
number of red-green line intersections inside the face.
Note that this number is independent on how we pair up the
(A_{r})_{e}=1
(
(A_{g})_{e}=1
) edges.

For example, in the 8-gon face shown below, we have 4
(A_{r})_{e}=1
edges (marked in thick red) and 2
(A_{g})_{e}=1
edges (marked in thick green).
The connecting lines are shown as thin red and green lines, and there is one intersection:

Thus, the cup product evaluates to

and the according path-integral weight is
e^{2\pi i\frac{1}{2}1}=-1
.

19

If there is an edge
e
with both
(A_{r})_{e}=1
and
(A_{g})_{e}=1
, it becomes ambiguous whether there is a red-green intersection at the edge center or not, which can be resolved by shifting the red and green edge centers with respect to another.
However, this case does not appear when showing the equivalence of the color and twisted cellular path integrals.

2D equivalence —

Let us now consider the 2D color path integral, which is a sum over color 1-cocycles
A
.
Using the chain map defined in Section
III.3
, we can turn
A
into a pair of cellular 1-cocycles
A_{r}\coloneqq M_{1}^{r}A
and
A_{g}\coloneqq M_{1}^{g}A
on the same 2-colex without the coloring.
We will now show that the actions are equivalent, i.e.,

\frac{1}{4}\sum_{p\in\Delta_{0}}\sgn_{p}\overline{A_{p}}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{f\in\Delta_{2}}(A_{r}\cup A_{g})(f)\;.

(82)

In fact, we will show the stronger statement that this equation holds locally:
It holds if we restrict the right-hand side to a single
b
-colored face
f
, and the left-hand side to the vertices
p\in f
:

\frac{1}{4}\sum_{p\in f}\sgn_{p}\overline{A_{p}}=\frac{1}{2}(M^{r}A\cup M^{g}A)(f)\;.

(83)

Note that (1) each vertex
p
is part of exactly one
b
-colored face, and (2)
M^{r}A
is only supported on the
\overline{r}
-colored edges, and
M^{g}A
only on the
\overline{g}
-colored edges, so the right-hand side is only non-zero on the
b
-colored faces where
rg
intersections can happen.
Thus summing the local equalities Eq. (
83
) over all
b
-colored faces yields Eq. (
82
).
To show Eq. (
83
), we notice that both sides are
0
if the number of vertices
p\in f
with
A_{p}=1
and
\sgn_{p}=+1
is equal to that with
A_{p}=1
and
\sgn_{p}=-1
, and
\frac{1}{2}
otherwise.
For the left-hand side, this is rather obvious.
For the right-hand side, we notice that every
A_{p}=1
vertex gives rise to one
(A_{r})_{e}=1
edge and one
(A_{g})_{e}=1
edge.
If
\sgn_{p}=+1
, then the
(A_{r})_{e}=1
edge is next to the
(A_{g})_{e}=1
edge in clockwise direction, otherwise their ordering is counter-clockwise.
Note that we start a red line from every
(A_{r})_{e}=1
edge center and a green line from every
(A_{g})_{e}=1
edge center.
If there is one clockwise-ordered pair of
(A_{r})_{e}=1,(A_{g})_{e}=1
edges and another counter-clockwise pair, then the green and red lines connecting them do not intersect.
More generally, the number of
rg
intersections is
0\operatorname{mod}2
if the number of clockwise pairs is equal to the number of counter-clockwise pairs, and
1\operatorname{mod}2
otherwise.

3D cellular path integral —

Let us now go back to the 3D color path integral and show that it is equivalent to the following
twisted cellular path integral
:

\displaystyle\begin{split}Z^{\text{cell}}=&\sum_{A_{r},A_{g},A_{b}\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\Delta_{1}}}\prod_{f\in\Delta_{2}}\delta_{(d^{\text{cell}}A_{r})_{f}=0}\;\delta_{(d^{\text{cell}}A_{g})_{f}=0}\\
&\times\delta_{(d^{\text{cell}}A_{b})_{f}=0}\prod_{v\in\Delta_{3}}e^{2\pi i\frac{1}{2}(A_{r}\cup A_{g}\cup A_{b})(v)}\;.\end{split}

(84)

So the path integral is the sum over all triples of cellular 1-cocycles
A_{r}
,
A_{g}
, and
A_{b}
, with an action

S[A_{r},A_{g},A_{b}]=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{v\in\Delta_{3}}(A_{r}\cup A_{g}\cup A_{b})(v)\;.

(85)

Again,
\cup
denotes is the cup product, and the value of the action on a volume
v
only depends on the values of
A_{r}
,
A_{g}
, and
A_{b}
on the edges of
v
.
On a tetrahedron with vertices labeled
0
,
1
,
2
, and
3
, and edges labeled accordingly by
01
,
02
,
03
,
12
,
13
, and
23
, the path-integral weight is given by the type-III group 3-cocycle
[
54
]

\omega\in Z^{3}(B\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{3},U(1))
:

\displaystyle\begin{multlined}\omega\Big(\big((A_{r})_{01},(A_{g})_{01},(A_{b})_{01}\big),\big((A_{r})_{12},(A_{g})_{12},(A_{b})_{12}\big),\\
\big((A_{r})_{23},(A_{g})_{23},(A_{b})_{23}\big)\Big)\end{multlined}

(86)

\displaystyle=(-1)^{(A_{r})_{01}(A_{g})_{12}(A_{b})_{23}}\;.

Intuitively,
A_{r}
,
A_{g}
, and
A_{b}
can be pictured as closed-membrane patterns,
A_{r}\cup A_{g}
is a closed-loop pattern formed by the intersection of
A_{r}
and
A_{g}
, and
A_{r}\cup A_{g}\cup A_{b}
is the set of points where this closed-loop pattern intersects with the closed-membrane pattern
A_{b}
.
In other words, the action counts the number of triple-intersections between the three closed-membrane patterns
A_{r}
,
A_{g}
, and
A_{b}
.
To make this intuition into a concrete formula, we need to make some local choices.
(1) We need to choose three distinct points on every edge, labeled
r
,
g
, and
b
.
(2) For every configuration of
A_{r}
on the edges of each face, choose a way to connect the
r
-points on the
A_{r}=1
-edges with “
r
” lines.
We make the analogous choices for
A_{g}
and
A_{b}
such that the
r-g
,
r-b
, and
g-b
intersection points are always distinct.
With these choices, we can compute
(A_{r}\cup A_{g}\cup A_{b})(v)
as follows:
The
r
lines inside every face
f\subset v
(for the corresponding
A_{r}
-configuration) together form a closed-loop pattern inside the boundary of
v
, and analogously for
g
and
b
.
Choose a “
r
” closed-membrane pattern inside the volume
v
whose boundary is the
r
closed-loop pattern, and analogously for
g
and
b
.
Now,
(A_{r}\cup A_{g}\cup A_{b})(v)
is the
\operatorname{mod}2
number of triple-intersections of the
r
,
g
, and
b
membranes inside the volume
v
.
Note that the number of triple-intersections is independent of the chosen membranes, since
v
is a 3-ball with trivial homology.

3D equivalence —

Having defined the twisted cellular path integral, let us now show that it is equivalent to the color path integral.
We translate the color 1-cocycle
A
summed in the color path integral into three
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
-valued cellular 1-cocycles
A^{r}\coloneqq M^{r}A
,
A^{g}\coloneqq M^{g}A
, and
A^{b}\coloneqq M^{b}A
.
Then, we show that the actions are equivalent, i.e.

\frac{1}{8}\sum_{p\in\Delta_{0}}\sgn_{p}\overline{A_{p}}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{v\in\Delta_{3}}(A^{r}\cup A^{g}\cup A^{b})(v)\;.

(87)

In fact, we show the stronger condition that this equation holds locally:
The equivalence also holds if we restrict to a single
y
-colored volume
v
on the right-hand side, and to all vertices of
v
on the left-hand side:

\frac{1}{8}\sum_{p\in v}\sgn_{p}\overline{A_{p}}=\frac{1}{2}(M^{r}A\cup M^{g}A\cup M^{b}A)(v)\;.

(88)

Note that (1) every vertex is adjacent to exactly one
y
-colored volume, and (2) the right-hand side is zero on every non-
y
-colored volume, since one of
M^{r}A
,
M^{g}A
, or
M^{b}A
is not supported there, and so there are no triple-
rgb
intersections inside these volumes.
Thus, summing Eq. (
88
) over all
y
-colored volumes yields Eq. (
87
).
To show Eq. (
88
), we start by noting that it holds if
A_{p}=0
for all
p\in v
, since both sides are zero.
Next, we note that the boundary of
v
is a 2-colex, and
A
defines a color 1-cocycle on this 2-colex.
Since the 2D color cohomology of a 2-sphere is trivial, any color 1-cocycle
A
can be obtained from
A=0
by applying gauge transformations
A^{\prime}=A+d_{\text{2D,color}}f
for different faces
f\subset v
.
Now, consider such a gauge transformation for a
by
-colored face
f\subset v
.
Then, we study how both sides of Eq. (
88
) change if we change
A
to
A^{\prime}
:

\displaystyle\begin{split}\frac{1}{8}\sum_{p\in v}&\sgn_{p}\overline{A_{p}^{\prime}}-\frac{1}{8}\sum_{p\in v}\sgn_{p}\overline{A_{p}}\\
\overset{\eqref{eq:integer_lift_expansion}}{=}&\frac{1}{8}\sum_{p\in v}\sgn_{p}(\overline{(df)_{p}}+2\overline{(df)_{p}}\overline{A_{p}})\\
=&\frac{1}{8}\sum_{p\in f}\sgn_{p}+\frac{1}{4}\sum_{p\in f}\overline{A_{p}}\overset{\eqref{eq:2dcolor_action_equivalence_helper}}{=}\frac{1}{2}(A^{r}\cup_{\text{2D}}A^{g})(f)\\
\overset{*}{=}&\frac{1}{2}((A^{\prime})^{r}\cup(A^{\prime})^{g}\cup(A^{\prime})^{b})(v)-\frac{1}{2}(A^{r}\cup A^{g}\cup A^{b})(v)\;.\end{split}

(89)

We find that they change by the same amount.
For the equation labeled (*), we have used that
(A^{\prime})^{r}=A^{r}
and
(A^{\prime})^{g}=A^{g}
, since each
\overline{r}
-colored or
\overline{g}
-colored edge shares two or no vertices with the
by
-colored face
f
.

(A^{\prime})^{b}
differs from
A^{b}
by all edges that share one vertex with
f
.
Thus, the closed-loop configurations on
v
for
(A^{\prime})^{b}
and
A^{b}
differ by a closed loop surrounding
f
.
Adding a closed loop around
f
to
A^{b}
leads to an additional triple-membrane crossing inside
v
precisely if
A^{r}
and
A^{g}
have an odd number of line crossings inside
f
, which is measured by
(A^{r}\cup_{\text{2D}}A^{g})(f)
.
Eq. (
89
) holds analogously if
f
has color
yr
or
yg
.
Since any color 1-cocycle
A
on the boundary of
v
can be obtained by a sequence of gauge transformations starting with
A=0
, Eq. (
88
) holds for all
A
.

IV.4
Flux and charge defects

In this section, we will equip the color path integral with
flux and charge defects
.
While the color path integral is equal to the twisted color circuit from Section
II
where all measurement outcomes are post-selected to
+1
, the color path integral with flux and charge defects correspond to the circuit post-selected onto some non-trivial configuration of outcomes.
Adding flux and charge defects is therefore essential for turning the path integral into a circuit of non-post-selected measurements, as well as for discussing decoding as in Section
V
.
Inserting flux and charge defects means modifying the path integral such that it depends on a
flux configuration

b
, and a
charge configuration

c
.

b
is a color 2-cochain on the 3-colex, and
c
is a color 1-chain.

Untwisted case: Definition —

We start by introducing flux and charge defects in the untwisted color path integral in Eq. (
75
):

Z_{\text{untw}}[b,c]=\sum_{A\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\Delta_{0}}:dA=b}\prod_{p\in\Delta_{0}}(-1)^{\frac{1}{2}A_{p}c_{p}}\;.

(90)

The flux and charge configurations modify the path integral in two ways:
First, instead of summing over all color 1-co
cycles

A
, we sum over all color 1-co
chains
whose boundary is the flux configuration,
dA=b
.
Second, there is an additional path-integral weight of
(-1)^{A_{p}c_{p}}
at every vertex
p\in\Delta_{0}
, which depends on the charge configuration.
20
20

20

Alternatively, we can interpret
c
as taking values in the Pontryagin dual
\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{*}
.
Then this weight is equal to the evaluation of
c
on
A
.

Note that we recover the original path integral for
b=0
and
c=0
,
Z_{\text{untw}}[0,0]=Z_{\text{untw}}
.

Untwisted case: Properties —

The flux and charge defects each obey two central properties, which are important for decoding and fault tolerance of the untwisted color circuits.
The first property is that the flux configuration must be a color 2-cocycle, otherwise the untwisted color path integral evaluates to zero:

db\neq 0\Rightarrow Z_{\text{untw}}[b,c]=0\;.

(91)

The simple reason for this is that if
db\neq 0
, then there exists no color 1-cochain
A
such that
dA=b
due to Eq. (
29
), so the summation in Eq. (
90
) is empty.
In fact, this equation holds locally, meaning that if
db\neq 0
at some location in the 3-colex, then the path integral evaluated on a small neighborhood of this location is zero.
Specifically, if
(db)_{(v,c)}\neq 0
for some volume
v\in\Delta_{3}
and color
c\neq\mathbf{c}_{v}
, then the path integral only on
v
is zero, where all
A_{p}
with
p\in v
are state-boundary variables.
The analogous property for the charges is that the charge configuration must be a color 1-cycle,

d^{T}c\neq 0\Rightarrow Z_{\text{untw}}[b,c]=0\;.

(92)

Again, this equation holds locally:
Assume that
(d^{T}c)_{v}\neq 0
on some volume
v
, and evaluate the path integral on any neighborhood such that all vertices
p\in v
are not boundary variables, and thus summed over.
Then, the summation over all color 1-cocycles
A
cancels:

\displaystyle\begin{split}Z_{\text{untw}}[b,c]=&\sum_{A}\prod_{p\in\Delta_{0}}(-1)^{A_{p}c_{p}}\\
=&\frac{1}{2}\sum_{A}\big(\prod_{p\in\Delta_{0}}(-1)^{A_{p}c_{p}}+\prod_{p\in\Delta_{0}}(-1)^{(A+dv)_{p}c_{p}}\big)\\
=&\frac{1}{2}\sum_{A}\prod_{p\in\Delta_{0}}(-1)^{A_{p}c_{p}}\big(1+\prod_{p\in\Delta_{0}}(-1)^{(dv)_{p}c_{p}}\big)\\
=&\frac{1}{2}\sum_{A}\prod_{p\in\Delta_{0}}(-1)^{A_{p}c_{p}}\big(1+\prod_{p\in v}(-1)^{c_{p}}\big)\\
=&\frac{1}{2}\sum_{A}\prod_{p\in\Delta_{0}}(-1)^{A_{p}c_{p}}\big(1+(-1)^{(d^{T}c)_{v}}\big)=0\;.\end{split}

(93)

The second property is that the path integral is invariant under adding the coboundary of a 1-chain
\beta
to
b
:

Z_{\text{untw}}[b+d\beta,c]\propto Z_{\text{untw}}[b,c]\;.

(94)

As usual, this holds locally:
If
\beta
consists of a single vertex
p^{\prime}
, then it holds for the path integral on a small neighborhood of
p^{\prime}
:

\displaystyle\begin{split}Z_{\text{untw}}[b+dp^{\prime},c]=&\sum_{A:dA=b+dp^{\prime}}\prod_{p\in\Delta_{0}}(-1)^{A_{p}c_{p}}\\
\overset{*}{=}&\sum_{A:dA=b}\prod_{p\in\Delta_{0}}(-1)^{(A+p^{\prime})_{p}c_{p}}\\
=&Z_{\text{untw}}[b,c]\prod_{p\in\Delta_{0}}(-1)^{(p^{\prime})_{p}c_{p}}\\
=&Z_{\text{untw}}[b,c](-1)^{c_{p^{\prime}}}\;.\end{split}

(95)

In the equation labeled
*
, we have performed a change of summation variable from
A
to
A+p^{\prime}
.
An analogous property holds for the charges:
The path integral is invariant under adding the boundary of a 2-chain
\gamma
to
c
:

Z_{\text{untw}}[b,c+d^{T}\gamma]\propto Z_{\text{untw}}[b,c]\;.

(96)

Again, this equation holds locally:
If
\gamma
consists of a single face
f
, then the equation holds for
Z
on a constant-size neighborhood of
f
:

\displaystyle\begin{split}&Z_{\text{untw}}[b,c+d^{T}f]\\
=&\sum_{A:dA=b}\prod_{p\in\Delta_{0}}(-1)^{A_{p}(c+d^{T}f)_{p}}\\
=&\sum_{A:dA=b}\prod_{p\in\Delta_{0}}(-1)^{A_{p}c_{p}}\prod_{p\in\Delta_{0}}(-1)^{A_{p}(d^{T}f)_{p}}\\
=&Z_{\text{untw}}[b,c](-1)^{(dA)_{f}}\\
=&Z_{\text{untw}}[b,c](-1)^{b_{f}}\;.\end{split}

(97)

Relation to anyons and 1-form symmetries —

The flux and charge configurations
b
and
c
can be viewed as
anomalous 1-form symmetry defects

[
28
,
57
,
58
]
in the untwisted color path integral.
Eqs. (
94
) and (
96
) make the defects “symmetric”.
The “anomaly” corresponds to the fact that the equations only hold up to a global prefactor, as shown in Eqs. (
95
) and (
97
).
The symmetries are “1-form” because color 2-cocycles and 1-cycles can be mapped to (three copies of) cellular 2-cocycles and 1-cycles, as shown in Section
III.3
.
These can be pictured as a closed-loop pattern inside the 3D spacetime.
In contrast, an ordinary global “0-form” symmetry would correspond to domain walls in spacetime, that is, closed-membrane pattern.
Physically, the closed loops in spacetime can be interpreted as anyon worldlines, and the
(-1)^{c_{\beta}}
and
(-1)^{b_{\gamma}}
factors in Eqs. (
95
) and (
97
) correspond to their braiding.

Defects and Pauli flows —

Let us briefly discuss what charge and flux defects look like if we describe the untwisted color path integral as a
ZX
tensor network as in Section
II
, and relate them to the formalism of
Pauli flows
(also called “Pauli webs” or “stabilizer flows”)
[
59
,
25
,
34
]
.
If a face
f
carries a flux defect,
b_{f}=1
, then this means that the path integral weight
\delta_{(dA)_{f}=0}
is replaced by
\delta_{(dA)_{f}=1}
.
Thus, this modified weight is represented by an
X
-tensor with a
\pi
-phase.
If a vertex
p
carries a charge defect,
c_{p}=1
, this corresponds to an additional weight
(-1)^{A_{p}}
, which can be implemented in the
ZX
diagram by adding a
\pi
-phase to the according
Z
-tensor.

In the context of
ZX
tensor networks, flux (charge) defects are related to
Pauli-
X
(Pauli-
Z
) insertions
.
A Pauli-
X
(Pauli-
Z
) insertion corresponds to a set of bonds in the tensor network, where we insert a Pauli-
X
(Pauli-
Z
) operator.
Note that Pauli-
Z
and
X
operators are 2-index
Z
and
X
-tensors with a
\pi
-phase,

\begin{gathered}\hbox to11.38pt{\vbox to44.57pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 5.69046pt\lower-20.96587pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1}

(100)

This is the tensor-network formulation of the invariance in Eq. (
94
) for
\beta=p
.
Analogously, we can add a
\pi
-phase to all the
X
-tensors at all the vertices around a face
f
, corresponding to the invariance in Eq. (
94
) for
\gamma=f
.

Now, we can also consider applying a set of invariances that leave
b
(
c
) unchanged, namely a set of vertices
\beta
(faces
\gamma
) which is a 1-cocycle with
d\beta=0
(or a 2-cycle with
d^{T}\gamma=0
).
Such sets of invariances are an example for
Pauli flows

[
59
,
25
,
34
]
, which have been used extensively for the construction of fault-tolerant circuits.
Pauli flows can be defined for an arbitrary
stabilizer tensor network
, whose tensors are stabilizer states
[
34
]
, and which is the kind of tensor network corresponding to circuits of Clifford gates and post-selected Pauli measurements.
Pauli flows are usually drawn by coloring each bond in the tensor network by the Pauli operator (
\{\mathbb{1},X,Y,Z\}
in general) that is inserted (and removed) at that bond during the application of the invariances.
In our
ZX
tensor network, the Pauli flows consist either purely of
X
, or of
Z
operators, which we color in red and blue, respectively.
For every volume
v
, there is one
X
Pauli flow given by
\beta=dv
.
That is,
\beta
consists of all vertices of
v
, and the Pauli flow is given by marking all bonds adjacent to the according
Z
-tensors in red.
Similarly, for each volume
v
and color
c\neq\mathbf{c}_{v}
, there is one
Z
Pauli flow with
\gamma=d^{T}(v,c)
.
That is,
\gamma
consists of all faces of
v
whose color does not contain
c
, and the Pauli flow is given by marking all bonds adjacent to the according
X
-tensors in blue.
Such local Pauli flows are called
detector flows
.
The following shows an example of the
X
detector flow, and one of the
Z
detector flows at a yellow volume in the 3-colex:

\includegraphics[width=85.35826pt,valign={c}]{figures/xdetector_flow.png}\quad,\qquad\includegraphics[width=56.9055pt,valign={c}]{figures/zdetector_flow.png}\;.

(101)

If we insert a Pauli-
Z
operator at a red edge of a (Pauli-
X
) detector flow, applying the according invariance yields a global factor of
-1
due to the anti-commutativity of
X
and
Z
.
The analogous holds when inserting a Pauli-
X
operator at a blue edge of a (Pauli-
Z
) detector flow.
In this sense,
X
detector flows (red) detect Pauli-
Z
(and
Y
) insertions and
Z
detector flows (blue) detect Pauli-
X
(and
Y
) insertions.
We find that any local Pauli insertion that is not equivalent to the trivial insertion via
ZX
rewrite rules, is detectable, and hence, the protocols have a macroscopic fault distance.
Note that this also is guaranteed more generally by the fixed-point property of the path-integral, which manifests in terms of linear constraints on the flux and charge configurations as discussed above.

Pauli flows also describe the logical action of a Clifford protocol
[
25
,
34
]
.
We have established that the local equivalences among Pauli insertions in the
ZX
diagram, that combine to Pauli flows, agree with 1-cocycle and 2-cycle condition in the color path integral.
This means that the
X
(
Z
) logical flows are given by non-trivial color 1-cocycles (2-cycles).

Twisted case: Definition —

Let us now return to the original, twisted, color path integral used to construct twisted color circuits.
For each non-trivial flux configuration
b
and charge configurations
c
we define a modified (twisted) color path integral, similar to the untwisted case,

Z[b,c]=\sum_{A\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\Delta_{0}}:dA=b}\prod_{p\in\Delta_{0}}e^{2\pi i(\frac{1}{8}\sgn_{p}\overline{A_{p}}+\frac{1}{2}A_{p}c_{p})}\;.

(102)

Note that we recover the color path integral in Eq. (
76
) for
b,c=0
.
Compared to the untwisted case, the properties in Eqs. (
91
), (
92
), (
94
) and (
96
) are modified due to the non-trivial action entering
Z[0,0]
.
Eq. (
91
) holds unchanged, since it only relies on the fact that
db=ddA=0
.
Eq. (
94
) does not hold anymore, and it is unclear whether there is a meaningful way to fix it.
Luckily, we do not need to rely on this property for fault tolerance.
The constraint and invariance in Eqs. (
92
) and (
96
) are modified in the twisted case in the presence of non-trivial flux,
b\neq 0
:
While the constraint in Eq. (
92
) gets replaced by a weaker constraint, the invariance in Eq. (
96
) can be extended to a stronger invariance.
Note that
b
and
c
correspond to configurations of measurement outcomes in the twisted color circuits, and the modified
c
constraints correspond to modified detectors generating a modified syndrome.
Using this modified syndrome may be important for effective decoding, as we discuss in Section
V
.
In the following we study these modified constraints, which we refer to as
twisted charge constraints
.

Twisted charge constraints —

As we saw earlier, the (generating) charge constraints correspond to detectors in the context of quantum error correction.
We will therefore refer to the generating twisted charge constraints as
twisted charge detectors
, and denote their set by
X
.
The twisted charge constraint is of the form

K^{b}d^{T}c=k^{b}\;,

(103)

where the matrix
K^{b}\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{X\times\Delta_{3}}
and the vector
k^{b}\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{X}
are defined as follows.
First, consider the symmetric matrix
M^{b}\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\Delta_{3}\times\Delta_{3}}
, defined by

M^{b}_{vv^{\prime}}=\sum_{f\in\Delta_{2},f\in v,v^{\prime}}b_{f}\;.

(104)

That is, if
v
and
v^{\prime}
do not share a face, then
M^{b}_{vv^{\prime}}=0
.
If they share a face
f
, then
M^{b}_{vv^{\prime}}
equals the value of
b
on
f
.
For
v=v^{\prime}
,
M^{b}_{vv}
is equal to the sum of
b
over all faces of
v
.

Given
M^{b}
,
K^{b}
can be chosen to be any maximum-rank matrix such that

(K^{b}M^{b})_{xv}=\sum_{v^{\prime}\in\Delta_{3}}K^{b}_{xv^{\prime}}M^{b}_{v^{\prime}v}=0\quad\forall x\in X,v\in\Delta_{3}\;.

(105)

In other words, we choose
K^{b}
such that the vectors
\{K^{b}_{x}\}_{x\in X}
form a complete basis for the kernel of
M^{b}
.
Finally, in order to define
k^{b}
, we need to choose a fixed
A_{0}
such that
dA_{0}=b
.
Then, we set

\displaystyle\begin{split}k^{b}_{x}\coloneqq&\frac{1}{2}\sum_{v\in\Delta_{3}}\sum_{p\in\Delta_{0},p\in v}(A_{0})_{p}K^{b}_{xv}\\
&+\sum_{v<v^{\prime}}M^{b}_{vv^{\prime}}K^{b}_{xv^{\prime}}K^{b}_{xv^{\prime\prime}}\;.\end{split}

(106)

The expression above takes integer values, as we show below, and is interpreted
\operatorname{mod}2
.

Before we verify that the twisted charge constraint in Eq. (
103
) indeed holds, let us discuss how it differs from the charge constraint in the untwisted color path integral.
First, we find that for every volume
v
such that
b_{f}=0
on all faces
f\in v
, we have
M^{b}_{vv^{\prime}}=0\forall v^{\prime}
.
Thus, each such volume
v
also gives rise to a twisted detector
x
with
K^{b}_{xv}=\delta_{x=v}
.
More generally, consider a connected component
V\subset\Delta_{3}
, where two volumes are considered connected if they share a face
f
with
b_{f}=1
.
Then, we have
M^{b}_{vv^{\prime}}=0\;\forall v\in V,v^{\prime}\neq V
.
Thus, we can choose a basis of twisted detectors, such that twisted detector is supported only on one connected component.
On a high level, the twisted charge constraint can be summarized as follows:
The volumes adjacent to a non-trivial flux face do not yield twisted charge detectors individually as in the untwisted case, but instead each connected component of such volumes together yields a small number of twisted charge detectors.

After stating the twisted charge constraints, let us now show that they hold.
We begin by defining the
gauge variance
of the action
S
,

\Delta S_{\alpha}[A]=S[A+d\alpha]-S[A]\;,

(107)

for any color 1-cocycle
A
and 0-cochain
\alpha
.
We find for any pair of volumes
v
and
v^{\prime}
,

\displaystyle\begin{split}\Delta S_{v+v^{\prime}}[A]-\Delta S_{v}[A]-\Delta S_{v^{\prime}}[A]\overset{\eqref{eq:gauge_variance_definition}}{=}&S[A+dv+dv^{\prime}]-S[A+dv]-S[A+dv^{\prime}]+S[A]\\
=&\frac{1}{8}\sum_{p}\sgn_{p}\big(\overline{(A+dv+dv^{\prime})_{p}}-\overline{(A+dv)_{p}}-\overline{(A+dv^{\prime})_{p}}+\overline{A_{p}}\big)\\
\overset{\eqref{eq:integer_lift_expansion}}{=}&\frac{1}{8}\sum_{p}\sgn_{p}\big(\overline{(dv^{\prime})_{p}}-2\overline{(A+dv)_{p}}\overline{dv^{\prime}}_{p}-\overline{(dv^{\prime})_{p}}+2\overline{A_{p}}\overline{(dv^{\prime})_{p}}\big)\\
\overset{\eqref{eq:integer_lift_expansion}}{=}&\frac{1}{4}\sum_{p}\sgn_{p}\big(-(\overline{A_{p}}+\overline{(dv)_{p}}-2\overline{A_{p}}\overline{(dv)_{p}})\overline{(dv^{\prime})_{p}}+\overline{A_{p}}\overline{(dv^{\prime})_{p}}\big)\\
=&\sum_{p}\sgn_{p}\big(-\frac{1}{4}\overline{(dv)_{p}}\overline{(dv^{\prime})_{p}}+\frac{1}{2}\overline{A_{p}}\overline{(dv)_{p}}\overline{(dv^{\prime})_{p}}\big)\\
\overset{*}{=}&\frac{1}{2}\sum_{p}\overline{A_{p}}\overline{(dv)_{p}}\overline{(dv^{\prime})_{p}}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{f:f\in v,f\in v^{\prime}}\sum_{p\in f}A_{p}\\
=&\frac{1}{2}\sum_{f:f\in v,f\in v^{\prime}}b_{f}=\frac{1}{2}M^{b}_{vv^{\prime}}\;.\end{split}

(108)

For the equality labeled (
*
), we have used that two volumes
v
and
v^{\prime}
share either no vertices
p
, or they share a face and all adjacent vertices.
Since each face has equal number of vertices with
\sgn_{p}=1
and
\sgn_{p}=-1
, the first term vanishes.
In words, the equation says that
\Delta S_{\alpha}[A]
, as a function of
\alpha
for a fixed
A
, is a
quadratic refinement

[
60
]
of the
\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}
-valued bi-linear form defined by the matrix
M^{b}
.
Using this, we find

\displaystyle\begin{split}\Delta S_{K^{b}_{x}}[A_{0}]\overset{\eqref{eq:quadratic_refinement}}{=}&\sum_{v}K^{b}_{xv}\Delta S_{v}[A_{0}]+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{v<v^{\prime}}M^{b}_{vv^{\prime}}K^{b}_{xv}K^{b}_{xv^{\prime}}\\
\overset{\eqref{eq:modified_detector_charge}}{=}&\frac{1}{2}k^{b}_{x}\;,\end{split}

(109)

using the notation
K^{b}_{x}\coloneqq\sum_{v}K^{b}_{xv}\cdot v
for the
x
th row of the matrix
K^{b}
.
We can now use Eq. (
108
) to show that (1)
k^{b}
is integral, and (2) it can only depend on the cohomology class of
A_{0}
.
For (1), we observe that

\displaystyle\begin{split}-2\Delta S_{K^{b}_{x}}[A_{0}]=&\Delta S_{0}[A_{0}]-\Delta S_{K^{b}_{x}}[A_{0}]-\Delta S_{K^{b}_{x}}[A_{0}]\\
\overset{\eqref{eq:quadratic_refinement}}{=}&\frac{1}{2}(K^{b}_{x})^{T}M^{b}K^{b}_{x}=0\;,\end{split}

(110)

which implies that
k^{b}_{x}=-2\frac{1}{2}k^{b}_{x}=0\operatorname{mod}1
, recalling that both equations above are in
\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}
.
For (2), we calculate

\displaystyle\begin{split}\Delta S_{K^{b}_{x}}[A_{0}+d\alpha]\overset{\eqref{eq:gauge_variance_definition}}{=}&\Delta S_{K^{b}_{x}+\alpha}[A_{0}]-\Delta S_{K^{b}_{x}}[A_{0}]\\
&-\Delta S_{\alpha}[A_{0}]+\Delta S_{K^{b}_{x}}[A_{0}]\\
\overset{\eqref{eq:quadratic_refinement}}{=}&\frac{1}{2}\alpha^{T}M^{b}K^{b}_{x}+\Delta S_{K^{b}_{x}}[A_{0}]\\
\overset{\eqref{eq:kmatrix_definition}}{=}&\Delta S_{K^{b}_{x}}[A_{0}]\;.\end{split}

(111)

To show the twisted charge constraint in Eq. (
103
), consider a patch of the spacetime 3-colex such that
K^{b}_{x}
is supported on its interior.
If
(K^{b}d^{T}c)_{x}\neq k^{b}_{x}
, then we find

\displaystyle\begin{split}Z[b,c]=&\sum_{A}e^{2\pi i(S[A]+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{p}A_{p}c_{p})}\\
=&\frac{1}{2}\big(\sum_{A}e^{2\pi i(S[A]+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{p}A_{p}c_{p})}\\
&+e^{2\pi i(S[A+dK^{b}_{x}]+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{p}(A+dK^{b}_{x})_{p}c_{p})}\big)\\
\overset{\eqref{eq:gauge_variance_definition}}{=}&\frac{1}{2}\sum_{A}e^{2\pi iS[A]}(1+e^{2\pi i(\Delta S_{K^{b}_{x}}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{p}(dK^{b}_{x})_{p}c_{p})})\\
\overset{\eqref{eq:twisted_constraint_offset_gaugevariance}}{=}&\frac{1}{2}\sum_{A}e^{2\pi iS[A]}(1+(-1)^{k^{b}_{x}+(K^{b}d^{T}c)_{x}})\\
=&\frac{1}{2}\sum_{A}e^{2\pi iS[A]}(1-1)=0\;.\end{split}

(112)

In addition to the weakened (twisted) constraints, the invariance in Eq. (
96
) can be extended:
For any locally supported 1-chain
\Gamma
such that
K^{b}d^{T}\Gamma=0
, we have

Z[b,c+\Gamma]\propto Z[b,c]\;.

(113)

This includes 1-chains of the form
\Gamma=d^{T}\gamma
, which form the invariance in the untwisted case.

Physical interpretation of twisted constraints —

Let us briefly discuss the physics interpretation of our findings.
The twisted constraint for the charge configuration in the (twisted) color path integral mirrors the fusion rules of the anyon theory of the underlying non-Abelian phase.
Recall that in Section
IV.3
, we showed the phase equivalence between the color path integral and the type-III twisted
\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{3}
Dijkgraaf-Witten state sum, whose anyon model is known
[
54
]
.
Using the cohomology mapping in Section
III.3
, we can generate special charge or flux configurations that look like isolated strings, which we can interpret as
anyon worldlines
.
Each of the three generating flux strings is associated with two non-Abelian anyons of quantum dimension
2
.
21
21

21

In fact, a flux string corresponds to the direct sum of both non-Abelian flux anyons.

The fact that the flux constraint in Eq. (
91
) is unchanged mirrors the fact that the fusion of two non-Abelian flux anyons of the same type always yields an anyon with trivial flux.
However, due to their non-Abelian nature, there is only a topological invariance for isolated flux worldlines, but no cohomological invariance for some (possibly dense) network of fluxes as for the untwisted case in Eq. (
94
).
22
22

22

If the fluxes in the model would correspond to Abelian worldlines, then the invariance in Eq. (
94
) can be rescued by adding further terms to the action as it was done in Ref.
[
28
]
.

The charge configuration still corresponds to a pattern of Abelian anyon worldlines in the path integral.
The fact that the charge constraint
d^{T}c=0
is weakened and does not need to hold on volumes with non-trivial flux faces mirrors the fact that the fusion of two non-Abelian fluxes can result in Abelian charges.
Or, in other words, the Abelian charge worldlines can terminate on the flux worldlines.

Charges and fluxes in 3D color code —

The color path integral is closely related to the 3D color code and its transversal
T
gate
[
31
]
, see Section
II
.
Let us briefly discuss to what kind of objects the charge and flux configurations and their constraints correspond in the 3D color code.
The flux configuration
b
corresponds to a
\pm 1
configuration of measurement outcomes of the
Z
stabilizers
S_{f}^{Z}
, or in other words, a
Z
syndrome or
Z
excitation of the 3D color code.
The charge configuration
c
, on the other hand, does not correspond to the syndrome for the
X
stabilizers
S_{v}^{X}
.
Rather, the operator acting as
Z^{c_{p}}
at every 3-colex vertex
p
maps the code state of the 3D color code to one with
X
syndrome given by
d^{T}c
.

Let us next study what happens if we apply the transversal
T
gate
\overline{T}=\prod_{p\in\Delta_{0}}T_{p}^{\sgn_{p}}
to a color-code state with
Z
syndrome
b
and
X
syndrome
d^{T}c

[
45
]
.
The action of the transversal
T
gate on the
X
syndrome is trivial, since the
Z^{c_{p}}
operator that creates it commutes with
T
.
It thus suffices to study the action on a state
\ket{b}
with a definite flux syndrome
b
but trivial charge syndrome.
After applying the
\overline{T}
gate,
\overline{T}\ket{b}
is an eigenstate of the conjugated
S^{X}
stabilizers

\displaystyle\widetilde{S}_{v}^{X}\coloneqq\overline{T}S_{v}^{X}\overline{T}^{\dagger}=\prod_{p\in v}S_{p}^{\sgn_{p}}X_{p},

(114)

where
S=i^{\outerproduct{1}{1}}
denotes the single-qubit Clifford phase gate.
In order to determine the
X
syndrome of
\overline{T}\ket{b}
, we measure the original stabilizers
S_{v}^{X}
.
If
S_{v}^{X}
and
\widetilde{S}_{v}^{X}
commute, then the measurement outcome will be deterministic, and if they anti-commute it will be fully random.
Computing the group commutator
\commutator{A}{B}_{G}\coloneqq ABA^{-1}B^{-1}
yields

\displaystyle\commutator{S_v^X}{\widetilde{S}_{v'}^X}_{G}=\prod_{f:f\in v,f\in v^{\prime}}S_{f}^{Z}.

(115)

Accordingly, we find

\displaystyle\begin{split}\bra{b}\prod_{f:f\in v,f\in v^{\prime}}S_{f}^{Z}\ket{b}=&(-1)^{\sum_{f:f\in v,f\in v^{\prime}}b_{f}}\\
=&(-1)^{M_{vv^{\prime}}^{b}}\;,\end{split}

(116)

recovering the quadratic form from Eq. (
108
) that describes the gauge variance.

S_{v}^{X}
will yield a deterministic outcome on
\overline{T}\ket{b}
exactly if it commutes with all
\widetilde{S}_{v^{\prime}}^{X}
, which is the case if
M^{b}_{vv^{\prime}}=0
for all
v^{\prime}
.
More generally, a product

\prod_{v\in\Delta_{3}}(S_{v}^{X})^{\alpha_{v}}

(117)

of generating
S_{v}^{X}
stabilizers yields a deterministic outcome if the vector
\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}^{\Delta_{3}}
is in the kernel of
M^{b}
.
So the subgroup of the original
X
-stabilizer group that yields deterministic outcomes is generated by

\left\{\prod_{v\in\Delta_{3}}K^{b}_{xv}S_{v}^{X}\right\}_{x\in X}\;,

(118)

using the matrix
K^{b}
from Eq. (
105
).
The deterministic outcome of the measurement does not have to be
+1
.
Instead, it is given by
k_{x}^{b}
from Eq. (
106
):

\prod_{v\in\Delta_{3}}K^{b}_{xv}S_{v}^{X}\overline{T}\ket{b}=(-1)^{k^{b}_{x}}\overline{T}\ket{b}\;.

(119)

Concretely, such deterministic
-1
outcomes can occur for configurations
b
consisting of linked loops, a phenomenon which was called
linking charge
in Ref.
[
45
]
.

IV.5
Boundaries

In this section, we revisit the boundaries of the path integral in Section
II.4
in more detail, and describe other constructions for topological boundaries.
In order to define a boundary condition for the color path integral, we need to (1) extend color cohomology to 3-colexes with boundaries, and (2) extend the action in Eq. (
77
) to the boundaries.
(1) and (2) need to satisfy two crucial conditions:
(1) the extension of color cohomology to the boundary needs to be locally exact, and (2) the extension of the action to the boundary needs to be gauge invariant.
We will here only state the different boundaries, and derive them explicitly in Appendix
A
.
There, we also discuss examples of boundaries in 2D and boundaries that do not fulfill local exactness or gauge invariance, and we show that we have found all possible boundaries using their equivalence to boundaries of a cellular twisted path integral.

Geometrically, we will define the boundaries on an arbitrary 2D surface formed by faces of the 3-colex.
For any such surface, we introduce the following notation:

•

\Delta_{i}^{\text{bd},c}
for
i=0,1,2
denotes the set of
i
-cells of the 3-colex that are part of the boundary and have coloring
c
.

•

\Delta_{3}^{\text{bdin},c}\subset\Delta_{3}
denotes the set of volumes that are adjacent to a boundary face.

•

\Delta_{3}^{\text{bdout},c}\not\subset\Delta_{3}
denotes the set of “phantom” volumes that are not part of the 3-colex, but adjacent to a boundary face on the “outside”.

•

\Delta_{2}^{\text{bdout}}\not\subset\Delta_{2}
denotes the set of “phantom” faces that are adjacent to one or more boundary edges in
\Delta_{1}^{\text{bd}}
but outside the boundary.

•

\Delta_{0}^{\text{bdout},c}\subset\Delta_{0}^{\text{bd}}
(
\Delta_{0}^{\text{bdin},c}\subset\Delta_{0}^{\text{bd}}
) denotes the set of boundary vertices that are adjacent to a single volume in
\Delta_{2}^{\text{bdout},c}
(
\Delta_{2}^{\text{bdin},c}
), which is of color
c
.

All-rough boundary —

The first boundary type is the
all-rough boundary
.
The generator sets of the boundary cohomology are

\displaystyle X_{0}

\displaystyle\coloneqq\Delta_{3}\;,

\displaystyle X_{1}

\displaystyle\coloneqq\Delta_{0}\;,

(120)

\displaystyle X_{2}

\displaystyle\coloneqq\Delta_{2}+\Delta_{2}^{\text{bdout}}\;,

\displaystyle X_{3}

\displaystyle\coloneqq\bigsqcup_{c\in\mathcal{C}_{1}}(\Delta_{3}^{c}+\Delta_{3}^{\text{bdout},c})\times\overline{c}\;,

and the boundary maps
d_{0}
,
d_{1}
,
d_{2}
are simple restrictions of these in the bulk.
The boundary action looks the same as the bulk one in Eq. (
77
), where the summation runs over all vertices
p\in\Delta_{0}
including those on the boundary.
The
ZX
tensor network for this boundary is discussed later in Section
VI
, where it is depicted in Fig.
23
.

Color boundary —

The second family of boundaries are
color boundaries
.
There are four such boundaries, one for every color
c
, where we set
c=r
(red) without loss of generality.
The cohomology theory is

\displaystyle X_{0}

\displaystyle\coloneqq\Delta_{3}-\Delta_{3}^{\text{bdin},r}+\Delta_{3}^{\text{bdout},g}+\Delta_{3}^{\text{bdout},b}+\Delta_{3}^{\text{bdout},y}\;,

(121)

\displaystyle X_{1}

\displaystyle\coloneqq\Delta_{0}\;,

\displaystyle X_{2}

\displaystyle\coloneqq\Delta_{2}-\Delta_{2}^{\text{bd},gb}-\Delta_{2}^{\text{bd},gy}-\Delta_{2}^{\text{bd},by}+\Delta_{1}^{\text{bd},\overline{r}}\;,

\displaystyle X_{3}

\displaystyle\coloneqq\bigsqcup_{c\in\mathcal{C}_{1}}\Delta_{3}^{c}\times\overline{c}\;.

d_{1}^{T}
maps an edge
e\in\Delta_{1}^{\text{bd},\overline{r}}
to both of its endpoints.

d_{2}
acts on an edge
e\in\Delta_{1}^{\text{bd},\overline{r}}
as follows:
First, we map
e
to all adjacent faces in
\Delta_{2}^{\text{bd},gb}
,
\Delta_{2}^{\text{bd},gy}
, and
\Delta_{2}^{\text{bd},by}
.
Then, we act on these faces with the bulk coboundary map
d_{2}
from Eq. (
49
).
Otherwise, the coboundary maps are restrictions of the bulk ones in Eq. (
49
).
The boundary action extends from Eq. (
77
) to the boundary as follows:

S^{\text{bd},r}[A]=\frac{1}{8}\sum_{p\in\Delta_{0}-\Delta_{0}^{\text{bdin},r}}\sgn_{p}\overline{A_{p}}\;.

(122)

This boundary is the one used in Section
II
.

Double-color boundary —

The third family of boundaries are
double-color boundaries
.
There are 6 such boundaries, one for each color pair
\kappa
.
Without loss of generality, we choose
\kappa=rg
.
The cohomology theory is

\displaystyle\begin{split}X_{0}\coloneqq&\Delta_{3}-\Delta_{3}^{\text{bdin},r}-\Delta_{3}^{\text{bdin},g}+\Delta_{3}^{\text{bdout},b}+\Delta_{3}^{\text{bdout},y}\;,\\
X_{1}\coloneqq&\Delta_{0}\;,\\
X_{2}\coloneqq&\Delta_{2}-\Delta_{2}^{\text{bd}}+\Delta_{2}^{\text{bd},rg}+\Delta_{1}^{\text{bd},\overline{r}}+\Delta_{1}^{\text{bd},\overline{g}}\;,\\
X_{3}\coloneqq&\bigsqcup_{c\in\mathcal{C}_{1}}\Delta_{3}^{c}\times\overline{c}+\Delta_{2}^{\text{bd},by}\;.\end{split}

(123)

d_{2}^{T}
maps a boundary face
f\in\Delta_{2}^{\text{bd},by}
to all of its edges.
Apart from this, the coboundary maps are defined similarly to Eq. (
121
).
The boundary action looks the same as in Eq. (
122
).
The according
ZX
tensor network is shown in Section
VI
in Fig.
23
.

In total, there are 11 distinct boundaries of the 3D twisted color path integral corresponding to three families, namely 1 all-rough, 4 color, and 6 double-color boundaries.

V
Decoding and fault tolerance

In this section, we discuss in more detail how to decode the twisted color circuit from Section
II
.
We describe decoding in five different steps:
In Section
V.1
we explain how to decode the untwisted color circuit without
T
gates.
In Section
V.2
, we discuss how the presence of
T
gates in the twisted color circuit makes it necessary decode and apply
X
corrections while running the circuit, and how this can be achieved using a
just-in-time
decoder.
While
Z
errors could be corrected in the same way as in the untwisted circuit, we show in Section
V.3
how the output of just-in-time
X
decoding can be used to improve the
Z
decoding of the twisted circuits.
In Section
V.4
, we discuss global aspects of the decoding procedure for a logical circuit using our non-Clifford logical elements.
We phrase the subroutines of the decoding problem in all these sections as hypergraph matching problems, for which we propose concrete (efficient) algorithms in Section
V.5
.

V.1
Decoding of the untwisted color circuits

Let us warm up by discussing how to perform decoding and corrections in the
untwisted
color circuits, where we omit the physical
T
gates.
Similarly to other circuits for Abelian topological phases, 2D toric code
[
2
]
, color code
[
61
,
62
,
30
]
, or honeycomb Floquet code
[
63
,
64
]
, it suffices to record all measurement outcomes while running the circuit, and decode at a later time.
This is the main difference to the
twisted
color circuits which we discuss in the following sections, where we need to perform decoding and corrections while executing the circuit.

Decoding in 3+0D —

Let us recall how decoding works for the 3+0D measurement-based protocol discussed in Section
II.2
, without the
T
gates.
For concreteness, we assume a 3-colex of the topology
S_{1}\times S_{1}\times[0,1]
, where the task is to reliably teleport the logical information from the input boundary
S_{1}\times S_{1}\times 0
to the output boundary
S_{1}\times S_{1}\times 1
.
After running the circuit and recording all measurement results, the task is to apply corrections to the output state such that it represents the logical state of the input.

Measurements in 3+0D —

We start by translating the measurement outputs into a flux configuration
b
and charge configuration
c
in the color path integral, as discussed in Section
IV.4
:
We recall that, if all
X
and
Z
measurement outcomes are
+1
, the post-selected circuit is equal to the untwisted color path integral as discussed in Section
II.2
.
If a
Z
measurement outcome at a face is
-1
, then this corresponds to adding a
\pi
phase to the

(127)

Equivalently, the
X
error contributes to the value of
b_{E}
on the four other faces.
All in all, an
X
(
Z
) error configuration can be represented as a
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
-valued vector
b_{\text{err}}
(
c_{\text{err}}
) with one entry for every location in the circuit where an error can occur.
The redistribution of
\pi
-phases above defines a local
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
-linear map which takes
b_{\text{err}}
(
c_{\text{err}}
) to a color 2-cochain
b_{E}
(1-chain
c_{E}
).
This map itself is not unique, as we can locally change
b_{E}^{\prime}=b_{E}+d\beta
(
c_{E}^{\prime}=c_{E}+d^{T}\gamma
) via the invariance in Eq. (
94
) (Eq. (
96
)).
However, the syndrome
db_{E}
(
d^{T}c_{E}
) is uniquely determined by
b_{\text{err}}
(
c_{\text{err}}
), due to
dd=0
.

Decoding algorithm in 3+0D —

The output state of the protocol at
S_{1}\times S_{1}\times 1
is not a color code state, but a state with
X
(
Z
) syndrome given by the termination of
b+b_{E}
(
c+c_{E}
) at the state boundary
S_{1}\times S_{1}\times 1
.
So we need to apply a correction that maps us back into the code space.
This correction is equal to inserting another flux (charge) configuration
b_{c}
(
c_{c}
) which is only supported near
S_{1}\times S_{1}\times 1
.
The whole circuit with measurements, errors, and corrections, forms a path integral with a total flux (charge) configuration given by
b+b_{E}+b_{c}
(
c+c_{E}+c_{c}
).
Due to the constraints in Eq. (
91
) (Eq. (
92
)), we know that this effective flux configuration
b+b_{E}+b_{c}
(charge configuration
c+c_{E}+c_{c}
) is a color 2-cocycle (1-cycle), otherwise measuring
b
(
c
) has zero probability.
Due to the invariance in Eq. (
94
) (Eq. (
96
)), a logical error occurs only if the effective flux (charge) configuration is (co)homologically non-trivial.
In other words, no logical fault occurs if we choose
b_{c}
(
c_{c}
) to be cohomologically equivalent to
b+b_{E}
(
c+c_{E}
).
Unfortunately, we do not know
b_{E}
(
c_{E}
), but only its syndrome
db_{E}=db
(
d^{T}c_{E}=d^{T}c
).
So the best we can do is to replace it with an estimate
\widetilde{b}
(
\widetilde{c}
) that also satisfies

d\widetilde{b}=db\;,\qquad(d^{T}\widetilde{c}=d^{T}c)\;.

(128)

It is the task of the decoder to find this estimate, and it succeeds if
\widetilde{b}
(
\widetilde{c}
) is cohomologically equal to
b_{E}
(
c_{E}
).
A strategy that generally works is to pick the
\widetilde{b}
(
\widetilde{c}
) fulfilling Eq. (
128
) with the smallest weight, or at least as small as we can find within runtime limitations.
Here, the weight is the number of faces
f
(vertices
v
) with
\widetilde{b}_{f}=1
(
\widetilde{c}_{p}=1
).
We will refer to the problem of low-weight finding solutions to Eq. (
128
) as
hypergraph matching
, and provide concrete algorithms in Section
V.5
.
Very roughly, the reason why this works is that for low enough error rate,
b_{E}
(
c_{E}
) has low weight with high probability, thus if we choose
\widetilde{b}
with low weight it will have the same (co)homology class than
b_{E}
(
c_{E}
) with high probability.
Finally, we note that the fault-tolerance argument can also be made for any arbitrary
p
-bounded local circuit-level noise model, without expressing it in terms of Pauli errors, which we do in Appendix
B
.

String-pattern picture —

After applying the mapping in Section
III.3
, coarse-graining and abstracting away the lattice, both
b
and
c
can be imagined as string patterns.
More precisely, each of
b
and
c
corresponds to 3 independent string patterns of three different colors.

db
and
d^{T}c
are the endpoints of these string patterns.

b_{E}
and
c_{E}
, as well as
\widetilde{b}
and
\widetilde{c}
are low-weight string patterns with the same endpoints.

b+\widetilde{b}
and
c+\widetilde{c}
are string patterns that are closed everywhere except for the points where they terminate on the output state boundary
S_{1}\times S_{1}\times 1
.

b_{c}
and
c_{c}
close off these termination points inside the output state boundary.

Decoding in 2+1D —

Decoding of a 2+1D untwisted color circuit (still without physical
T
gates) works essentially in the same way as described above for the 3+0D protocol.
There are a few small differences which we list below.
First, we do not get all the measurement outcomes at the same time, but we record them over time to then perform decoding at a later time step.
This may be either when we pass the logical information into some other gadget that requires a clean corrected state, or when determining the classical outcome of a logical measurement, which is encoded in the charge configuration.

Measurement outcomes in 2+1D —

The second difference is that there is no one-to-one correspondence between individual
Z
-type (
X
-type) measurement outcomes in the circuit and the flux (charge) value at an individual face (vertex) in the 3-colex.
Instead, the history of all
Z
measurement outcomes (
X
measurement outcomes) form a
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
-valued vector
b_{\text{meas}}
(
c_{\text{meas}}
), which is related to the flux configuration
b
(charge configuration
c
) by a local
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
-linear map, just like the relation between
b_{\text{err}}
and
b_{E}
(
c_{\text{err}}
and
c_{E}
) above.
Again,
b
(
c
) is only defined up to local 2-coboundaries (1-boundaries), but its syndrome
db
(
d^{T}c
) is uniquely determined by
b_{\text{meas}}
(
c_{\text{meas}}
).

To get a map between
b_{\text{meas}}
and
b
(
c_{\text{meas}}
and
c
), we express the
-1
-post-selected projectors of each measurement in the circuit as a
ZX
diagram, and move the corresponding
\pi
-phases to the nearby tensors.
Let us give a few examples of this map for the circuit in Fig.
3
discussed in Section
II
.
The
-1

\pi
-phase through part of the
CX
gate yields a third
\pi
-phase:

(134)

At most other places in the circuit, a single-qubit
X
or
